topStories.headline: Five Months In, SoMa's $19M RESET Center Is Running at Less Than 30% Capacity — and Neighbors Say the Streets Feel the Same
topStories.dek: A new SF Standard analysis finds the Sixth Street sobering center has logged roughly 450 admissions per month since May, far below its stated goal of 2,500 — while a longtime SoMa resident says conditions outside have not visibly improved.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's RESET Center at 444 Sixth Street in SoMa opened on May 4, 2026, as Mayor Daniel Lurie's signature drug-enforcement alternative — a place where people arrested for public intoxication could sober up in reclining chairs under medical supervision instead of cycling through the county jail or emergency rooms. The $19 million converted warehouse, run by Connections Health Solutions under Sheriff's Office oversight, was designed to process as many as 2,500 people per month.

Five months into operations, however, a San Francisco Standard analysis published October 1 found the center has logged about 2,250 total admissions — roughly 450 per month — and is operating at less than 30 percent of its potential scale. Daily admissions more than doubled between July and September, rising from about 10 to 21 per day, but the facility's 25 reclining chairs — with an average stay of 7.5 hours — have the capacity to serve more than 75 people daily.

For SoMa West residents, the street-level measure is what they see outside. Leah Edwards, who has lived in SoMa for more than a decade and is treasurer of the SoMa West Neighborhood Association, told the Standard she hasn't noticed a difference in street conditions since the center opened. The SoMa West CBD's September newsletter separately noted that "questions remain regarding RESET connections for incapacitated individuals and program outcome metrics."

District 6 Supervisor Matt Dorsey, who championed the center and co-sponsored its enabling legislation, has said the city planned to scale up gradually. The RESET pilot also arrives alongside a new jurisdictional change: as of October 1, Southern Station's patrol boundaries expanded north to Market Street — adding an estimated 23 percent more calls for service — putting fresh pressure on staffing that was already a flashpoint for neighborhood groups.

topStories.headline: Wrecking Ball Coffee Plans a Potrero Hill Cafe This December and a Dogpatch Roastery by 2027
topStories.dek: The Bay Area specialty roaster, which shrank to a single Cow Hollow shop during the pandemic, is expanding with two new cafes and a dedicated roasting facility — and two of the three sites are in these neighborhoods.
topStories.body:
Wrecking Ball Coffee Roasters, the San Francisco specialty coffee company founded by Trish Rothgeb in 2011, is mounting a significant comeback after the pandemic forced it down to a single storefront. The SF Standard reported on September 24 that Wrecking Ball plans to open a second cafe at 1700 20th Street in Potrero Hill in December 2026, a third cafe at 3030 Telegraph Avenue in Berkeley, and a standalone roasting facility in Dogpatch expected to debut in late 2027.

The expansion is backed by two new co-owners who joined the company at the close of 2025. Wrecking Ball once operated two San Francisco cafes and a roastery on Folsom Street, but contracted sharply during COVID-19; roasting has since been handled by a third party. Hoodline, citing the Standard's original reporting, noted the story was published September 26.

Rothgeb is a significant figure in the specialty coffee world — she is credited with coining the term "third-wave coffee" in 2002. The Dogpatch roastery is described as the most ambitious piece of the expansion: a dedicated production facility that would bring roasting back in-house. No address for that location has been announced publicly. The Potrero Hill cafe at 1700 20th St. is the only opening currently expected within the ten-week window, with a December 2026 target date.

topStories.headline: Treasure Island Density Expansion Still Awaits Board of Supervisors Sign-Off as Developer Eyes End-of-Year Deadline
topStories.dek: Developer TICD is seeking approval to add up to 2,800 units beyond the existing 8,000-unit cap, but the proposal still requires Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors action before December 31.
topStories.body:
The push to significantly expand housing on Treasure Island remains active this fall, with the developer — Treasure Island Community Development (TICD) — pressing for final Board of Supervisors approval before the end of 2026. A February 11 informational presentation to the Treasure Island Development Authority (TIDA) Board outlined a proposal to add between 1,400 and 2,800 residential units beyond the current 8,000-unit cap, while maintaining the existing 27.2 percent affordable housing requirement and 5 percent inclusionary rate.

The Board of Supervisors took up the item in a televised hearing on April 21, 2026, where the proposal's range and affordable-unit implications were reviewed. Per a San Francisco Chronicle report from January 2026, the amendment will require approval from both the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors, and TICD has said it needs final adoption by year's end to take advantage of near-term market conditions.

Meanwhile, the first phase of the broader Treasure Island build-out has already delivered tangible results: 490 Avenue of the Palms, a six-story, 148-unit condominium complex, opened in July 2026 as the island's first condo building, according to SF YIMBY. The project at full build-out calls for up to 10,000 homes at final density, 300 acres of parks and open space, and a population of more than 18,000 residents. SFMTA, which approved on-street metered parking for Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island in March 2026, is currently developing an implementation plan for that program alongside TIDA.

events.title: SF Fleet Week 2026 — Air Show, Parade of Ships & Ship Tours

moreNews.headline: Berry Street Closed to Vehicles in Mission Bay on October 7 for Sewer Upgrade Work
moreNews.body: SF Water Power Sewer is conducting Channel Force Main upgrades that will close Berry Street to vehicle traffic between 4th and 7th streets on Wednesday, October 7, 2026 from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pedestrian access will be maintained throughout. The Mission Bay TMA Shuttle is adjusting its West Route and Transbay/Caltrain stops for the day: the West Route stop at Berry & King will move to Berry & 5th, and the Transbay Route stop at Berry & King and Berry & Mission Creek will relocate to 185 Berry Street, in front of Lobby 6.

moreNews.headline: TIDA Appoints Sheela Jivan as New Executive Director of Treasure Island Development Authority
moreNews.body: City Administrator Carmen Chu appointed Sheela Jivan as Executive Director of the Treasure Island Development Authority (TIDA), effective May 7, 2026, according to the sf.gov city announcement. The appointment follows the January 2026 retirement of longtime director Robert Beck, who served more than 30 years in public service. Jivan is charged with bolstering economic and community development on the island, including overseeing ongoing housing, open space, and mixed-use projects as the buildout enters its next stage.
moreNews.sourceName: City and County of San Francisco
